title: Group 2 — Risk factors
text:
Spine

How do bodies carry risk, how do class and smoke talk, and where do children still die young?



Introduction — the tables we own
This folder is ours for the ten days. Three tables, three shapes.

Panel A (panel-A.csv) — cardioRiskFactors: BMI, lipids, blood pressure, uric acid. sex and smok have already been recoded from integers to factors.
Panel B (panel-B.csv) — Scottish Health Survey 1998: sex, social class, smoking, diagnosed CVD. area is a code, not a map.
Panel C (panel-C.csv) — SOWC child / infant / neonatal mortality by country. Join by country name.

If a brick needs a histogram, it lives in A. If it needs a mosaic, it lives in B.

library(tidyverse)
library(mosaic)
library(skimr)
library(ggformula)

A <- read_csv("data/panel-A.csv")
B <- read_csv("data/panel-B.csv")



Panel A — body / measure

bmi, choles, sys, dia, Uric are Quant. Do not average smok.

On the Qual variables, panel-A data has:

sex has 2 levels: “female” (524) and “male” (474)
smok has 2 levels: “non_smoker” (775) and “smoker” (223)
The split inside sex is very uneven: only 36 women smoke (vs 488 who don’t), while 187 men smoke (vs 287 who don’t)

On the Quant variables, panel-A data has:

age: mean 44.6, sd 11.5, median 45, min 25, max 64. Pretty flat, no skew.
bmi: mean 25.8, sd 5.3, median 25.1, min 14.8, max 48.6. Skewed right.
hdl: mean 1.54, sd 0.45, median 1.48. Slightly skewed right.
ldl: mean 3.45, sd 1.22, median 3.42. Close to symmetric.
sys: mean 135.9, sd 23.9, median 132, max 245. Skewed right.
Uric, trig, alco: very skewed right with a long tail (Uric goes up to 1885).
alco: 721 of 998 people have 0, so most people don’t drink at all.

There is no missing data.

A_mod <- A |> mutate(sex = as.factor(sex), smok = as.factor(smok))

glimpse(A_mod)

A few helper columns for later bricks. These are cut-offs we chose, not columns in the data: “high bp” is sys >= 140 or dia >= 90, “obese” is bmi >= 30, “drinker” is alco > 0.

A_flag <- A_mod |>
  mutate(
    high_bp = (sys >= 140 | dia >= 90),
    obese   = (bmi >= 30),
    drinker = (alco > 0)
  )

A_flag |> summarise(
  pct_high_bp = mean(high_bp),
  pct_obese   = mean(obese),
  n_nondrinkers = sum(!drinker)
)

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  pct_high_bp pct_obese n_nondrinkers
        <dbl>     <dbl>         <int>
1       0.484     0.197           721


Findings from this look:

524 women and 474 men; 775 non-smokers and 223 smokers (only 36 women smoke, compared to 187 men).
Most people don’t drink: 721 of 998.
48% of people have high blood pressure.
20% of people are obese (bmi >= 30).



2. Ask
Based on the spine, these are our questions:
Possibly can answer:

Are women and men affected differently? Do they carry risk in different ways?
Is waisthip a better match for risk markers than bmi? (Where you carry weight vs how much.)
Do smokers and non-smokers have different hdl and ldl levels, for men and for women? Is the pattern still there for non-drinkers? (Main Character Question)

Possibly cannot answer:

How much smoking matters. (No dose or duration of smoking, just smoker / non-smoker.)
Did any of these people get heart disease? (No outcome column, so we can’t tell whether a “high” value actually leads to heart disease.)



3. Choose a mark

Bar chart for the Qual counts (sex, smok), no histograms for these.
Histograms for single Quant variables (age, bmi, sys, alco, …)
Scatter + straight-line smoother for Quant + Quant (sys ~ age, sys ~ waisthip, sys ~ bmi, hdl ~ trig, hdl ~ alco), with a correlation number to back it up
Violins for Quant + Qual (2 levels): body measures by sex, and hdl / ldl by smok, split by sex
Density plot to see hdl and ldl side by side in one chart
Two-sample test for means beside the matching violin



4. Predict

Question 1: Men will carry more weight around the middle (waisthip), even if women have the higher bmi.
Question 2: waisthip will line up with blood pressure and uric acid more closely than bmi does.
Question 3 (Main Character): Smokers will have worse cholesterol: lower hdl and higher ldl than non-smokers.



5. Make
These are the charts we used to explore the data. They don’t show up in the render, but they helped us decide what to look at next.

## Qual counts
A_mod |> gf_bar(~ sex)
A_mod |> gf_bar(~ smok)
A_mod |> gf_bar(~ smok, fill = ~ sex)

## Quant shapes
A_mod |> gf_histogram(~ age)
A_mod |> gf_histogram(~ bmi)
A_mod |> gf_histogram(~ sys)
A_mod |> gf_histogram(~ Uric)
A_mod |> gf_histogram(~ alco)

Question 1: do women and men carry risk differently?

A_mod |> gf_violin(bmi ~ sex, fill = ~ sex) |>
  gf_labs(title = "Women have the higher BMI...", x = NULL)







A_mod |> gf_violin(waisthip ~ sex, fill = ~ sex) |>
  gf_labs(title = "...but men carry more weight around the middle", x = NULL)







A_mod |> gf_violin(sys ~ sex, fill = ~ sex) |>
  gf_labs(title = "Men have higher blood pressure", x = NULL, y = "Systolic BP (mmHg)")







A_mod |> gf_violin(Uric ~ sex, fill = ~ sex) |>
  gf_labs(title = "Men have much higher uric acid", x = NULL, y = "Uric acid")








Prediction was right: women have higher bmi, men have higher waisthip, blood pressure and Uric.
Blood pressure rises with age:

A_mod |> gf_point(sys ~ age) |> gf_smooth(method = "lm") |>
  gf_labs(title = "Blood pressure goes up with age", y = "Systolic BP (mmHg)")








Question 2: where you carry weight (waisthip) vs how much (bmi)

A_mod |> gf_point(sys ~ waisthip) |> gf_smooth(method = "lm")







A_mod |> gf_point(sys ~ bmi) |> gf_smooth(method = "lm")







A_mod |> gf_point(Uric ~ waisthip) |> gf_smooth(method = "lm")







A_mod |> gf_point(Uric ~ bmi) |> gf_smooth(method = "lm")







A_mod |> gf_point(trig ~ waisthip) |> gf_smooth(method = "lm")







A_mod |> gf_point(trig ~ bmi) |> gf_smooth(method = "lm")







# put numbers on it
cor(sys ~ waisthip, data = A_mod)

[1] 0.3270939

cor(sys ~ bmi, data = A_mod)

[1] 0.2147511

cor(Uric ~ waisthip, data = A_mod)

[1] 0.4902608

cor(Uric ~ bmi, data = A_mod)

[1] 0.1108893

cor(trig ~ waisthip, data = A_mod)

[1] 0.3892571

cor(trig ~ bmi, data = A_mod)

[1] 0.2192494


waisthip wins every time: sys 0.33 vs 0.21, Uric 0.49 vs 0.11, trig 0.39 vs 0.22.
More triglycerides, less HDL:

A_mod |> gf_point(hdl ~ trig) |> gf_smooth(method = "lm") |>
  gf_labs(title = "More triglycerides, less good cholesterol")








Drinkers have higher uric acid:

A_flag |> gf_violin(Uric ~ drinker, fill = ~ drinker) |>
  gf_labs(title = "Drinkers have higher uric acid", x = "Drinks alcohol?")







A_flag |> group_by(drinker) |> summarise(mean_Uric = mean(Uric), n = n())

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  drinker mean_Uric     n
  <lgl>       <dbl> <int>
1 FALSE        298.   721
2 TRUE         414.   277


Question 3 (Main Character): smokers and cholesterol, men and women separately
Human brick first: our own starting chart, before any AI.

# Our first attempt: HDL and LDL as two separate graphs
A_mod |> gf_histogram(~ hdl, fill = ~ smok, position = "dodge", bins = 25) |> gf_facet_wrap(~ factor(sex))
A_mod |> gf_histogram(~ ldl, fill = ~ smok, position = "dodge", bins = 25) |> gf_facet_wrap(~ factor(sex))

Problem: two separate graphs, so it’s hard to compare HDL and LDL side by side.

# ## Prompt we actually used
# "how can I plot these 2 graphs together so I can analyse both hdl and ldl side by side"

# ai_draft
A_mod |>
  pivot_longer(c(hdl, ldl), names_to = "cholesterol", values_to = "level") |>
  gf_density(~ level, fill = ~ smok, alpha = 0.5) |>
  gf_facet_grid(cholesterol ~ factor(sex))

# ours
# kept pivot_longer() + gf_facet_grid(), tried it as a histogram first,
# switched to density because the groups are really uneven (36 vs 488 women),
# added a title + caption


A_mod |>
  pivot_longer(c(hdl, ldl), names_to = "cholesterol", values_to = "level") |>
  gf_density(~ level, fill = ~ smok, alpha = 0.5) |>
  gf_facet_grid(cholesterol ~ sex) |>
  gf_labs(
    title = "Male smokers have more good cholesterol and less bad; women barely differ",
    caption = "Panel A, cardioRiskFactors (n = 998). Only 36 women smoke.",
    x = "Cholesterol (mmol/L)"
  )








The same comparison as violins, with the group means:

A_mod |> gf_violin(hdl ~ smok, fill = ~ smok) |> gf_facet_grid(~ sex) |>
  gf_labs(title = "Male smokers have higher good cholesterol (HDL)", x = NULL,
          caption = "Only 36 women smoke, so the female smoker violin is thin on data.")







A_mod |> gf_violin(ldl ~ smok, fill = ~ smok) |> gf_facet_grid(~ sex) |>
  gf_labs(title = "Male smokers have lower bad cholesterol (LDL)", x = NULL)







A_mod |> group_by(sex, smok) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_hdl = mean(hdl), mean_ldl = mean(ldl), .groups = "drop")

# A tibble: 4 × 5
  sex    smok           n mean_hdl mean_ldl
  <fct>  <fct>      <int>    <dbl>    <dbl>
1 female non_smoker   488     1.55     3.70
2 female smoker        36     1.51     3.46
3 male   non_smoker   287     1.45     3.39
4 male   smoker       187     1.68     2.89


The male smokers stand out: higher hdl, lower ldl. That’s the opposite of what we predicted. What else is different about them? Check drinking:

A_flag |> filter(sex == "male", smok == "smoker") |>
  summarise(pct_drinkers = mean(drinker))   # about 68%

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  pct_drinkers
         <dbl>
1        0.679

A_mod |> gf_point(hdl ~ alco) |> gf_smooth(method = "lm") |>
  gf_labs(title = "Good cholesterol rises a little with alcohol")








hdl rises with alco. So is it the smoking, or the drinking riding along with it? Repeat the comparison for non-drinkers only:

A_nd <- A_flag |> filter(!drinker)

A_nd |> gf_violin(hdl ~ smok, fill = ~ smok) |> gf_facet_grid(~ sex) |>
  gf_labs(title = "Non-drinkers only: male smokers still have higher HDL", x = NULL)







A_nd |> gf_violin(ldl ~ smok, fill = ~ smok) |> gf_facet_grid(~ sex) |>
  gf_labs(title = "Non-drinkers only: male smokers still have lower LDL", x = NULL)

6. Say

Prediction missed. Male smokers have higher hdl (about 0.24 higher on average) and lower ldl (about 0.5 lower) than male non-smokers, both p-values far below 0.05.
The pattern is still there among men who don’t drink (hdl about 0.23 higher, ldl about 0.5 lower), so drinking alone doesn’t explain it. Among women the gap is small, and only 36 women smoke.
Women carry risk differently from men: higher bmi in women; higher waisthip, blood pressure and Uric in men.
Blood pressure rises with age, and waisthip lines up with the risk markers (Uric, trig, sys) more closely than bmi does.
48% of this group has high blood pressure, 20% is obese, and 721 of 998 don’t drink.



7. Limit

We can’t say how much smoking matters: we only have smoker / non-smoker, no amount or duration.
We can’t say whether anyone got heart disease. There’s no outcome column, so a “high” value can’t be turned into “more likely to get heart disease”.
“High blood pressure”, “obese” and “drinker” are cut-offs we chose, not columns in the data.
This is one sample of 998 people. Associations here are not causes: a smoker’s higher hdl is not a reason to smoke.
Only 36 women smoke, too few to be sure about women.
We don’t know who these people are, where they’re from, or how they were chosen.
ldl is calculated from choles, hdl and trig, not measured on its own.
Some values are extreme (dia up to 172, Uric up to 1885).
Kit table we refused to abuse: smok and sex were never averaged or put in a histogram.


A_mod |> gf_histogram(~ choles, fill = ~ sex)

`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value `binwidth`.

Panel B — category / talk

smoke × sex, cvd × sc (social class). area is forbidden as geography. Do not average sc.


1. See the table

Our Panel-B data has:

B_mod <- B |>
  mutate(across(where(is.character), as.factor)) |>
  mutate(

                    "I-II (high)" = "12",
                    "III (middle)" = "3",
                    "IV-V (low)" = "45"),
    sc = fct_relevel(sc, "I-II (high)", "III (middle)", "IV-V (low)"),
    smoke = fct_relevel(smoke, "nevr", "ex", "lite", "mod", "hvy"),
    area = as.factor(area)

2. Ask
Based on the spine (how do class and smoke talk), these are our questions:
Possibly can answer:

Does higher social class (sc) go with lower deprivation (carstair)?
Is deprivation related to CVD?
Does social class affect CVD?
Does smoking lower your risk of CVD? (Main Character Question)

Possibly cannot answer:

Why do ex-smokers have the highest rate of CVD? Did they quit because they got ill? (No dates for quitting or diagnosis.)



3. Choose a mark

Bar chart for the Qual counts (sex, sc, smoke, cvd)
Boxplot for Quant + Qual (carstair by sc, carstair by cvd, age by smoke)
Mosaic plot for Qual + Qual (deprivation × sc, cvd × sc, smoke × cvd), shaded to show surprises
Chi-square test beside each mosaic: are two categories linked, or is it chance?
t-test (2 groups)

Question 1: Higher social classes will live in less deprived areas.
Question 2: Deprivation and CVD will be inversely related.
Question 3: Lower social classes will have more CVD.

6. Say

Class and place talk: higher social classes live in less deprived areas (class I–II average carstair -1.24 vs +0.65 for class IV–V, p far below 0.05).
More deprived areas have slightly more CVD (25% vs 29%), the opposite direction from our prediction. Small, but real.
Social class on its own barely changes CVD (p ≈ 0.06). Class shows up in where people live and how much they smoke more than in CVD directly.
Smoking does not lower your risk. Current smokers have about the same CVD rate as never-smokers, and ex-smokers have the most (36%), but they’re also the oldest group.



7. Limit

One snapshot from 1998. Links, not causes.
We don’t know when people quit smoking or when CVD was diagnosed, so some ex-smokers may have quit because they got ill.
smoke is in groups, and we don’t know what “lite” or “hvy” actually means in cigarettes.
carstair describes the area, not the person: a well-off person in a deprived area gets the area’s score.
sc is based on job type, which leaves out people without a job and says nothing about income.
cvd is just yes / no, with no type or severity.
Age affects almost everything here, and we haven’t fully separated it out.
The deprivation groups are cut-offs we chose (equal thirds).
Kit table we refused to abuse: sc and area were never averaged or treated as numbers, and area was never used as a map.




Conclusion

The spine so far: Bodies carry risk differently by sex (A), class talks to where people live and how much they smoke more than to heart disease directly (B), and smoking keeps refusing to behave the way we predicted in both panels.
The questions we will defend in ninety seconds:

Panel A: Do smokers and non-smokers carry cholesterol differently, and why do male smokers look healthier?
Panel B: Does smoking lower your risk of CVD? (No: ex-smokers have the most CVD, and they’re also the oldest.)

What we will not claim: that smoking is good for cholesterol or the heart, that social class causes CVD, or that anything here causes heart disease.
Which lines were human, which were machine:

Human: the questions in both panels, the predictions, the first HDL/LDL histograms, the sys/dia scatter, using facet_wrap() by sex, spotting the “how many cigarettes” limit, the helper columns and cut-offs, the violins and tally() counts, the cholesterol-by-sex histogram and t-test from class, the carstair histogram faceted by smoke, and the smoke × cvd mosaics and chi-square test.
Machine (AI-assisted): the pivot_longer() combined chart,, formatting index.qmd into the template layout, merging drafts into one file, formatting Panel B, the deprivation groups (cut_number()), the age check for ex-smokers, and checking the numbers in both panels.

Limits: one snapshot each, smoking is yes / no only in A and in loose groups in B, only 36 female smokers in A, age tangled up with smoking in B, carstair describes the area not the person, unknown sampling.
Gift for the steal-this strip: pivot_longer() to put two measures side by side in one faceted chart, helper columns with cut-offs stated out loud, and fct_relevel() / fct_recode() to put categories in a sensible order with readable names.
